Learning Objectives
Review the relevant pathoanatomy for common sports injuries about the ankle.
Discuss the relevant surgical anatomy for commonly performed sports medicine procedures
about the ankle.
List structures at risk during open and arthroscopic surgical procedures performed on the
ankle.
Osteology
Overview
The ankle, or tibiotalar joint, is formed by the tibia, fibula, and talus (Figure 1).

The tibiotalar joint is broadly categorized as a ginglymus, or hinge-type joint.
The distal tibia and fibula create a semirigid osseoligamentous housing, or mortise, for the
talus.
The talar dome is a biconcave articular surface with a central trochlea that is congruent with
the slightly convex distal tibial articular surface, providing additional intrinsic osseous
stability to the joint.
All three osseous contributions to the tibiotalar joint—tibia, fibula, and talus—include an
articular cartilage surface.
Figure 1 Lateral (A) and anterior (B) view illustrations show the lateral ankle and subtalar
ligaments. (Reproduced from Katcherian D: Soft-tissue injuries of the ankle, in Lutter LD, Mizel
MS, Pfeffer GB, eds: Orthopaedic Knowledge Update: Foot and Ankle. Rosemont, IL, American
Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 1994, pp 241-253.)

Overview
The ankle joint, also referred to as the tibiotalar or talocrural articulation, is formed by
the tibia, fibula, and talus. Mechanically, the joint is classified as a ginglymus, or hinge-
type joint; however, in reality the tibiotalar joint has complex, multiplanar motion
conferred by its osseoligamentous constraints.1 The ankle mortise, created by the distal
tibia and fibula, is semirigid, given the ligamentous contributions of the distal tibiofibular
syndesmosis laterally, whereas the medial malleolus is a direct osseous extension of the
distal tibia medially. The distal tibia, fibula, and talus all have articular cartilage
contributions creating tibiotalar, talofibular, and tibiofibular articulations.2 The mortise
creates a housing for the talus, yielding a mortise and tenon construct. Additional
inherent stability is conferred by the geometry of the talar dome,3 which is biconcave

with a central trochlear sulcus and is highly congruent with the convex distal tibia
articular surface in the coronal plane (Resources 1 and 2).
Distal Tibia
The distal tibia is covered by articular cartilage with a medial osseous extension, the medial
malleolus, that creates the medial pillar of the ankle mortise.
The distal tibial articular surface often is referred to as the plafond, or ceiling, of the ankle
mortise.
Almost the entire distal tibia, including the articular portion of the medial malleolus, is
covered by articular cartilage. The exception is a small anterior-to-posterior segment at the
junction of the plafond and the medial malleolus.4
In the sagittal plane, the plafond has a concave shape and accommodates the dome of the
talus.
In the coronal plane, the plafond has a subtle convexity that articulates with the trochlea of
the talus and divides the distal tibial articular surface into a medial and lateral facet.
The length of the arc of the articular surface of the plafond is shorter than the articular arc of
the dome of the talus, leaving portions of the talar dome uncovered in all positions of
motion.
The medial malleolus consists of an anterior and posterior colliculus. The anterior colliculus
projects more distally than the posterior colliculus.
An osseous groove on the posterior aspect of the medial malleolus houses the posterior
tibial tendon (PTT).
In the axial plane, the lateral border of the distal tibia has a concave groove referred to as the
incisura fibularis tibiae, or simply incisura, that becomes shallower proximally.5

Distal Tibia
The distal tibia contributes the ceiling and medial pillar of the ankle mortise. The distal
tibial articular surface, or plafond, is concave in the sagittal plane and slightly convex in
the coronal plane. The central convexity of the plafond in the coronal plane divides the
articular surface into medial and lateral articular facets. The articular arc length of the
plafond in the sagittal plane is shorter than that of the adjacent dorsal surface of the

9/3/26, 7:18 AM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004079

talar dome. Therefore, at any point during sagittal plane motion, a portion of the talar
dome articular surface is uncovered. The medial malleolus is an extension of the distal
tibia that creates the medial pillar. Its lateral surface is covered by articular cartilage that
articulates with the medial aspect, or auricular facet, of the talar dome. At the junction
between the medial facet of the plafond and the articular surface covering the medial
malleolus, a small, linear region that is not covered by articular cartilage frequently is
present, which is important to consider in performing surgical procedures such as
medial malleolar osteotomy.4 The anterior and posterior colliculi are terminal osseous
extensions of the medial malleolus. The anterior colliculus extends almost 0.5 cm more
distally than the posterior colliculus.6 The colliculi are separated by the intercollicular
groove, which, in combination with the colliculi, provide a broad surface for the origins of
the deep and superficial components of the deltoid ligament. The posterior aspect of the
medial malleolus has a consistent retromalleolar groove in the axial plane. The groove
provides an osseous constraint for the PTT. Soft-tissue extensions from the edge of the
groove create a fibro-osseous tunnel through which the PTT traverses the ankle,
maintaining stability of the tendon throughout ankle range of motion. On the lateral side
of the tibial plafond, a small, 3- to 9-mm proximal extension of the lateral facet articular
cartilage is present, which extends into the incisura fibularis tibiae and contributes to the
articular contact zone at the distal tibiofibular syndesmosis.5 Incisura morphology is
variable7 but generally is a well-defined concavity distally, becoming shallower
proximally. The concavity is defined by an anterior tubercle (the Chaput tubercle) and
posterior tubercle (the Volkmann tubercle).5 These tubercles correspond with the
insertions of the anterior-inferior tibiofibular ligament (AITFL) and the posterior inferior
tibiofibular ligament (PITFL) on the tibia, respectively.
Distal Fibula
The fibula terminates laterally at the lateral malleolus, which creates the lateral pillar of the
ankle mortise through the stout ligamentous attachments of the syndesmosis.
The medial aspect of the lateral malleolus has a triangular-shaped articular cartilage surface
that articulates with the lateral talus.6
A small, proximal extension of the articular surface of the fibula provides a small area of
articulation, or contact zone, between the fibula and the tibia at the distal extent of the

syndesmosis.5
Ligamentous attachments of the syndesmosis and lateral ankle ligament complexes attach to
multiple bony projections surrounding the articular surface of the lateral malleolus.
The posterior border of the fibula has a grooved surface for the peroneal tendons referred to
as the peroneal sulcus. The depth of the osseous sulcus is highly variable and may exist as a
flat or convex surface rather than a concave groove.8

Distal Fibula
The distal fibula terminates at the lateral malleolus. The lateral malleolus creates the
lateral pillar of the ankle mortise. Dissimilar from the medial pillar, which is a direct
osseous extension, the lateral pillar is maintained by stout, osseoligamentous
attachments of the distal tibiofibular syndesmosis. The medial aspect of the distal fibula
is covered in a triangular segment of articular cartilage that articulates with the trigonal
articular surface of the lateral talus.6 Similar to the tibia, a proximal projection of this
articular cartilage contributes to the articular contact zone at the distal tibiofibular
syndesmosis.5 Multiple, subtle osseous projections surround the articular cartilage of
the fibula and are present on the posterior, lateral, and anterior surface of the lateral
malleolus ; these projections correspond to ligamentous attachments of the lateral
ligament complex, distal tibiofibular ligaments, and superior peroneal retinaculum. The
posterior aspect of the lateral malleolus has a variably grooved surface to house the
peroneal tendons. At the lateral aspect of this groove, the superior peroneal retinaculum
originates and confers additional stability to the peroneal tendons as they traverse the
ankle joint.
Talus
The talus rests within the mortise created by the distal tibia and the fibula.
The talus articulates with all portions of the ankle mortise, yielding the tibiotalar articulation,
while also contributing to the subtalar and talonavicular articulations.
Approximately 60% of the talar surface is covered by articular cartilage.

The talus is the only tarsal bone without muscular or tendinous insertions. Stability is
conferred by the osseous morphology of the mortise and the ligamentous attachments.
The talus is morphologically categorized into the body, neck, and head.6 The talar body
includes the talar dome, which is the articular surface within the mortise.
The dorsal surface of the talar dome includes a medial and lateral facet separated by a subtle
trochlear sulcus.
The anterior aspect of the talar dome is wider in the coronal plane than the posterior aspect.
In combination with tensioning of the deltoid ligament during ankle dorsiflexion, this
geometry confers greater stability of the talus within the mortise in dorsiflexion compared
with plantar flexion.
The lateral facet of the talar dome has a larger radius of curvature than the medial facet,
creating a conical shape that narrows from lateral to medial.6
The articular surface of the talar dome extends medially—to include the auricular facet,
which articulates with the medial malleolus—and laterally—to include the trigonal articular
surface, which articulates with the lateral malleolus.6
The posterior process of the talus includes the posterolateral and posteromedial tubercles,
which yield a groove for the flexor hallucis longus (FHL) tendon.
The osseous anatomy of the posterolateral tubercle is highly variable and may exist as a
prominent trigonal process, often referred to as a Stieda process, or as an os trigonum9
(Resource 3; Figure 2).


Talus
The talus rests within the mortise and has no direct tendinous or muscular attachments.
Stability of the talus, and therefore the tibiotalar articulation, is conferred by the osseous
morphology of the mortise and the ligamentous attachments. Most of the talus, almost
60%, is covered by articular cartilage that includes the tibiotalar articulation and the
subtalar and talonavicular articulations. The talar body, which includes the talar dome, is
the primary component of the talus involved in ankle articulation. The talar dome is
wider anteriorly than posteriorly and has a longer lateral facet than medial facet. In the
sagittal plane, the articular arc of the talar dome is longer than that of the adjacent tibial
plafond, leaving a portion of the talar dome cartilage uncovered at any point of ankle
motion. The medial and lateral aspects of the talar dome also are covered in articular

cartilage and include the auricular and trigonal facets, respectively. Although not covered
in articular cartilage, the relationship of the talar dome and the talar neck may influence
some ankle conditions, such as anterior ankle impingement.10 The posterior process of
the talus includes a posterolateral and posteromedial tubercle. Together, the tubercles
create a groove for the FHL tendon as it obliquely traverses the posterior aspect of the
ankle. The posterolateral tubercle of the posterior process may have variable anatomy.
An elongated and intact posterolateral tubercle is continuous with the body of the talus
and is referred to as a trigonal process or Stieda process. In as many as 20% of patients,9
an elongated posterolateral tubercle is connected to the body of the talus by only a
fibrous or cartilaginous synchondrosis. This accessory bone is referred to as an os
trigonum. Although consistently described as an accessory bone in the literature, it is
better described as a failure of fusion of a secondary ossification or, less frequently, a
true stress fracture. The secondary ossification center that forms the posterolateral
tubercle typically is fused by age 13 years, and speculation exists that certain plantar
flexion activities, such as ballet, may stress the fusion process and result in a higher
prevalence in certain groups.11 Although most os trigonum are asymptomatic, they may
result in a subset of posterior ankle impingement syndrome referred to as os trigonum
syndrome.9
Ligaments
Lateral Ankle Ligament Complex
The lateral ankle ligament complex includes the anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL),
calcaneofibular ligament (CFL), and posterior talofibular ligament (PTFL).
The ATFL originates on the anterolateral surface of the lateral malleolus and inserts on the
lateral surface of the talar dome, just distal to the anterior margin of the trigonal facet. The
ATFL is a short, broad ligament that exists almost as a capsular thickening. It often exists as
two parallel bands (Figure 3). Strain in the ATFL increases with plantar flexion, inversion, and
internal rotation.
The CFL originates just anterior to the tip of the lateral malleolus and inserts on the lateral
wall of the calcaneus. It runs deep to the peroneal tendons and crosses the subtalar joint.
The CFL is a more distinct, cord-like ligamentous structure compared with the ATFL. The CFL
is under increased strain with dorsiflexion and inversion.

The PTFL originates on the medial surface of the lateral malleolus just posterior to the
articular cartilage and runs horizontally. It widens as it courses medially before inserting
broadly on the posterior aspect of the talar body, including distinct insertion on the
posterolateral tubercle of the posterior process. Its proximal border is continuous with the
posterior capsule of the ankle.12


Lateral Ankle Ligament Complex
The lateral ankle ligament complex includes the ATFL, CFL, and PTFL.
The ATFL is a wide, short, trapezoidal shaped ligament that is relatively indistinct and
may be considered a capsular thickening of the anterolateral ankle joint capsule (Figure
3). The ligament originates on the anterolateral surface of the lateral malleolus and
passes horizontally before inserting just distal to the articular cartilage of the talus at the
junction of the talar body and neck.

The CFL is a relatively distinct, cord-like ligamentous complex. It also originates on the
anterior surface of the lateral malleolus and extends distally to insert variably on the
lateral wall of the calcaneus posterior to the peroneal tubercle.
The PTFL originates on the medial surface of the lateral malleolus just posterior to the
trigonal articular cartilage surface. It broadens as it inserts medially on the posterior
aspect of the talus, with distinct insertions on the posterolateral tubercle.
Distal Tibiofibular Syndesmosis Ligament Complex
The distal tibiofibular syndesmosis ligament complex, or simply the syndesmosis, consistently
includes the AITFL, PITFL, and interosseous ligament, which expands into the interosseous
member proximally.
The stout ligamentous attachments, in combination with the osseous anatomy of the distal
fibula and the incisura, create a dynamic yet stable lateral column of the ankle mortise.
The AITFL originates on the Chaput tubercle of the tibia and courses obliquely over the
anterolateral ankle to insert on the Wagstaffe tubercle of the fibula, blending with the
proximal portion of the ATFL origin (Figure 4).

The AITFL typically has two to three distinct bands. The most distal band may become
redundant and thickened with chronic or recurrent syndesmotic injury and cause
anterolateral soft-tissue ankle impingement.13
Posterior to the AITFL fibers is a small, synovial recess adjacent to the articular cartilage of
the contact zone of the distal tibiofibular syndesmosis. Just proximal to the synovial recess is
the interosseous ligament.
The PITFL originates along the medial surface of the lateral malleolus, just posterior to the
articular cartilage. It courses obliquely to the posterior malleolus of the tibia, or the
Volkmann tubercle.
The PITFL has a superficial and deep component. Throughout the literature, the deep
component of the PITFL is variably referred to as a separate ligament, the transverse
ligament, or the posterior transverse ligament. It should not be confused with the
intermalleolar ligament, which is a distinct posterior capsular thickening between the
malleoli14,15 (Figure 5).

Distal Tibiofibular Syndesmosis Ligament Complex
The distal tibiofibular syndesmosis ligament complex creates a dynamic, yet stable
osseoligamentous connection for the lateral column of the ankle mortise. The
syndesmosis ligament complex includes the AITFL, PITFL, and interosseous ligament,
which expands into the interosseous member proximally. The AITFL originates on the
Chaput tubercle of the tibia and inserts on the Wagstaffe tubercle of the anterior fibula,
taking an oblique course over the anterolateral aspect of the ankle. With repetitive
injury, the distal fascicles of the AITFL may become redundant or thickened, which may
result in anterolateral ankle impingement syndrome. This was first described by Dr.
Frank Bassett as an accessory ligament,13 but it is best considered abnormal because of
recurrent or chronic injury. Posterior to the AITFL and within the concavity of the tibial
incisura is the articular cartilage contact zone between the distal tibia and fibula, with an
associated synovial recess. Interosseous ligamentous connections, specifically the
interosseous ligament, begin just proximal to this synovial recess and expand into the
interosseous membrane more proximally.5 Posteriorly, the PITFL runs horizontally

across the posterior aspect of the ankle, originating from the Volkmann tubercle of the
posterior tibia and inserting on the medial aspect of the lateral malleolus just behind the
triangular articular cartilage.12 The PITFL has distinct superficial and deep components,
the deep component extending the posterior lip of the tibial plafond as a labral-like
structure. The deep component of the PITFL may be separately referred to as the
transverse ligament or the posterior transverse ligament.14 It should not be confused
with the intermalleolar ligament, which is a capsular thickening of the posterior ankle
capsule, as it has been suggested in previous literature.15
Deltoid Ligament
The deltoid ligament on the medial aspect of the ankle includes the superficial and deep
components and works in combination with the syndesmosis to maintain the talus within the
mortise while resisting external rotation forces.The superficial and deep components of the
deltoid ligament originate broadly along the colliculi and intercollicular groove of the medial
malleolus.
The superficial deltoid fibers have multiple named but indistinct fascicles that insert broadly
on the navicular and sustentaculum tali (Figure 6).
The deep component of the deltoid is divided into anterior and posterior components, both
of which insert in the recess distal to the auricular facet of the medial talus.
The posterior component of the deep deltoid is the strongest portion of the deltoid ligament.
The deltoid ligament serves as the floor of the fibro-osseous tunnel for the PTT and the flexor
digitorum longus (FDL) tendon.12

Deltoid Ligament
The deltoid ligament works in combination with the syndesmosis to prevent external
rotation of the talus within the mortise. It is easily divided into superficial and deep
components. The superficial fibers of the deltoid have been variably named but exist as
relatively indistinct sheets of tissue despite the multiple names given to them. The fibers
originate from the medial aspect of the medial malleolus and the associated colliculi and
insert on the navicular and the sustentaculum tali.12 The deep component of the deltoid
ligament has more clearly defined anterior and posterior components. The posterior
component of the deep deltoid is considered the strongest portion of the ligament.
Combined with the anterior widening of the talar dome in the coronal plane, tensioning

the posterior component of the deep deltoid confers increased stability of the talus
within the mortise with ankle dorsiflexion. In addition to providing ligamentous
restraints, the deltoid serves as the floor of the fibro-osseous tunnels for the traversing
PTT and FDL.
Arterial Blood Supply
Arteries
Three large, named arteries typically traverse the ankle before entering the foot.
The posterior tibial artery crosses the posteromedial ankle with the medial flexor tendons.
Along with the tibial nerve, it is located directly anterior and medial to the FHL tendon at the
level of the ankle. Distally, it bifurcates into the medial and lateral plantar arteries beneath
the sustentaculum.
The peroneal artery has a prominent anterior perforating branch at the level of the distal
interosseous member and the interosseous ligament that creates a variable anastomosis
with the anterior tibial artery before forming the dorsalis pedis artery.
The anterior tibial artery runs between the tibialis anterior and the extensor hallucis longus
(EHL) tendon as it descends toward the ankle. At the level of the inferior extensor
retinaculum, the anterior tibial artery forms the dorsalis pedis artery and moves lateral to
the EHL tendon.
Blood Supply of the Talus
Given that no muscular or tendinous origins or insertions are present on the talus and that
almost 60% of its surface is covered by articular cartilage, vascular access to the bone is
limited.
The talar neck has little articular cartilage; therefore, a consistent anastomotic ring of vessels
surround the talar neck.
The anastomotic ring around the talar neck is formed by variable contributions from the
artery of the tarsal sinus, artery of the tarsal canal, and direct branches from the dorsalis
pedis artery.16
Because of the presence of the consistent anastomotic ring around the talar neck, it was
assumed that most of the blood supply to the talar body was retrograde, contributing to high

Recent studies using gadolinium-enhanced MRI have reported a predominant blood supply


Blood Supply of the Talus
Blood supply to the ankle is provided by contributions from the posterior tibial artery,
peroneal artery, and anterior tibial artery. The posterior tibial artery crosses the
posteromedial ankle with the medial flexor tendons; it courses directly anterior to the
tibial nerve, at which they are interposed between the FHL tendon posteriorly and the
FDL tendon anteriorly. During posteromedial approaches to the ankle or endoscopic
management of the posterior ankle, working lateral to the FHL tendon provides a
relatively safe zone to avoid injury to the posterior tibial artery. The peroneal artery
exists as a perforating branch proximal to the ankle joint and creates an anastomotic
network with the anterior tibial artery and the dorsalis pedis artery at the anterior ankle.
The anterior tibial artery proximal to the ankle courses between the tibialis anterior and
EHL muscle bellies. As it crosses the anterior ankle, the EHL tendon crosses over the
anterior tibial artery; therefore, the artery courses lateral to the EHL tendon as it enters
the foot and becomes the dorsalis pedis artery. All three of these major arteries provide
blood supply to the talus, which, because of its unique anatomic location, has historically
been studied as a result of its high rate of osteonecrosis.17 Although the tarsal sinus
artery, tarsal canal, and branches of the dorsalis pedis artery contribute to the much-
discussed anastomotic ring around the talar neck,16 recent studies have suggested that
a good portion of the blood supply to the talar body may be provided in an antegrade
fashion via contributions from the posterior tibial artery.18

complications and in considering their involvement as sources of pain. These purely sensory

The deep peroneal nerve runs within the anterior compartment proximal to the ankle
adjacent to the anterior tibial artery.
Proximal to the ankle, the deep peroneal nerve runs between the tibialis anterior and EHL
muscle bellies.
At the level of the ankle joint, the deep peroneal nerve divides into medial and lateral
branches.
The deep peroneal nerve branches enter the foot as they cross deep to the proximal border
of the inferior extensor retinaculum. At this location, a compression neuropathy of the deep
peroneal nerve can occur and is referred to as anterior tarsal tunnel syndrome.19
The posterior tibial nerve runs within the deep posterior compartment proximal to the ankle.
At the level of the ankle, the posterior tibial nerve courses just medial to the FHL tendon on
the posteromedial aspect of the ankle (Figure 8).
Along with the medial flexor tendons, the posterior tibial nerve crosses the ankle within the
tarsal tunnel formed by the posterior aspect of the medial malleolus, medial aspect of the
talus and calcaneus, and overlying flexor retinaculum.19

Mixed Motor and Sensory Nerves
Sensory and motor components of the tibial and peroneal nerves cross the ankle joint.
Knowledge of this anatomy is important for several reasons. First, predictable areas of
nerve compression may result clinically in entrapment neuropathies. Notable sites of
compression include the superficial peroneal nerve at its fascial exit from the lateral
compartment approximately 12 cm proximal to the tip of the lateral malleolus, the deep
peroneal nerve at the proximal border of the inferior extensor retinaculum, and the
posterior tibial nerve within the tarsal tunnel.19 More importantly, evolving surgical
techniques around the ankle put several of these structures at risk. For example, the
most common complication during ankle arthroscopy is injury to the intermedial dorsal
cutaneous branch of the superficial peroneal nerve during establishment of the
anterolateral ankle arthroscopy portal.21 Knowledge of this anatomic relationship and
foot positioning techniques to avoid injury to the intermedial dorsal cutaneous branch of
the superficial peroneal nerve22 is important for sports surgeons interested in ankle
arthroscopy. In addition, iatrogenic injury to the sural nerve as it courses distally
between the lateral border of the Achilles tendon and the peroneal tendons has been

Tendons Crossing the Ankle
Compartments of the Leg
The muscles of the leg exist within well-defined fascial compartments that develop into
tendinous structures that then cross the ankle joint in predictable locations (Table 1).
The anterior compartment contains the tibialis anterior, EHL, extensor digitorum longus, and
peroneus tertius muscles.
To prevent bowstringing and ineffective mechanics, the superior and inferior extensor
retinaculum contain the tibialis anterior, EHL, extensor digitorum longus, and peroneus
tertius tendons as they cross the ankle anteriorly.
The superficial posterior compartment contains the gastrocnemius and soleus muscles and
the plantaris muscle.
The gastrocnemius and soleus terminate as the Achilles tendon insertion on the posterior
tuberosity of the calcaneus. The plantaris tendon runs separately along the medial aspect of
the Achilles tendon and inserts on the medial aspect of the tuberosity or the medial wall of
the calcaneus.
The deep posterior compartment contains the tibialis posterior, FDL, and FHL, which become
entirely tendinous as they enter the ankle.
Posterior to the medial malleolus, the posterior compartment structures enter the fibro-
osseous tarsal tunnel.
Oriented from anteromedial to posterolateral in the tarsal tunnel are the PTT, FDL tendon,
posterior tibial artery, tibial nerve, and FHL tendon.
The lateral compartment contains the peroneus longus and the peroneus brevis. Both
tendons cross the ankle in a well-defined fibro-osseous tunnel posterior to the fibula.

Tarsal Tunnel
The contents of the tarsal tunnel include the PTT, FDL, and FHL tendons in addition to the
posterior tibial nerve and artery.
The retromalleolar groove containing the PTT serves as the anterior border of the tarsal
tunnel.
The posteromedial aspect of the talus, including the posterior process and tubercles
adjacent to the FHL tendon, in combination with the medial border of the calcaneus serve as
the floor of the tarsal tunnel.
The flexor retinaculum serves as the roof of the tarsal tunnel.
Peroneal Grove and Retinaculum
Peroneal tendon stability is conferred by a relatively shallow, occasionally convex, groove
along the posterior aspect of the fibula23 (Resource 5).
The peroneus brevis tendon is directly adjacent to the fibrocartilaginous groove with the
peroneus longus tendon posterior to the peroneus brevis.
The peroneal groove is formed anteriorly by the osseous peroneal groove on the fibula. The
floor of the groove is created by the CFL, and the superior peroneal retinaculum serves as
the roof of the groove.

The superior peroneal retinaculum originates from the posterior surface of the lateral
malleolus at the lateral aspect of the peroneal groove and runs superficial to the peroneal
tendons before variably inserting on the lateral wall of the calcaneus and the aponeurosis
continuous with the Achilles tendon posteriorly.
At the location at which the superior peroneal retinaculum originates on the posterior
surface of the lateral malleolus, a fibrocartilaginous lip deepens the fibro-osseous groove.
Given the variable anatomy of the osseous groove, the superior peroneal retinaculum
confers most of the stability to the peroneal tendons during ankle motion.
Distal to the lateral malleolus, the peroneal tendons run within a synovial sheath before
running deep to the inferior peroneal retinaculum at the level of the peroneal tubercle. The
peroneus brevis tendon is dorsal to the peroneal tubercle, whereas the peroneus longus
runs plantar to the peroneal tubercle.
Accessory Muscles
Various accessory muscles have been described about the ankle with variable clinical
consequence.24
A peroneus quartus muscle is present in 10% to 15% of individuals, originating from the
lateral compartment and continuing within the peroneal groove before inserting variably on
the lateral wall of the calcaneus or the peroneus longus tendon.
An accessory soleus is present in as many as 5% of individuals. The muscle originates in the
superficial posterior compartment adjacent to the normal soleus origin before inserting
along the dorsal calcaneus or the medial calcaneus.
The flexor digitorum accessorius longus is present in as many as 8% of individuals. It has a
variable origin within the deep posterior compartment before inserting on the quadratus
plantae or the FDL tendon.
The peroneocalcaneus internus is present in approximately 1% of individuals. It originates
from the fibula and courses lateral to the FHL in a parallel course before inserting at the base
of the sustentaculum tali on the medial calcaneus.

The muscles of the compartments of the leg give rise to the tendons crossing the ankle.
The tendons most intimately associated with the ankle come from the anterior, lateral,

and deep posterior compartments. Although the superficial posterior compartment
contents cross the ankle posteriorly, they are anatomically not intimately associated with
the joint. The anterior compartment tendons, including the tibialis anterior, EHL,
extensor digitorum longus, and peroneus tertius, cross the anterior ankle by passing
deep to the superior and inferior extensor retinaculum. The retinacular structures
prevent bowstringing of the tendons during ankle motion, maintaining a mechanical
advantage for foot and ankle motion. The tendons of the deep posterior compartment,
including the PTT, FDL, and FHL, pass along the posteromedial talus and are contained
within the tarsal canal. The lateral compartment tendons, including the peroneus longus
and brevis, are contained within the peroneal groove. The peroneal groove is defined by
the often-shallow groove on the posterior fibula, superior peroneal retinaculum (roof),
and CFL (floor). Given the shallow nature of the peroneal groove, the superior peroneal
retinaculum and associated fibrocartilaginous lip at its origin are important stabilizers of
the peroneal tendons. Injury to the superior peroneal retinaculum, in isolation or
associated with lateral ankle instability, may result in peroneal tendon instability.
Accessory muscles about the foot and ankle are relatively rare; however, their presence
may result in clinical symptoms, particularly if the accessory muscles occupy space in the
tarsal tunnel or the peroneal groove.
